stem: A 59-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to crushing chest pain accompanied by sweating and lightheadedness.  Blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and pulse is 48/min.  ECG shows sinus bradycardia and ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.  Occlusion of which of the following coronary arteries is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌
explanation:
This patient has chest pain and associated symptoms (eg, diaphoresis, lightheadedness) concerning for acute coronary syndrome, and ECG confirms ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).  In STEMI, the ECG leads demonstrating ST-segment elevation correspond with the affected region of the heart; leads II, III, and aVF are inferior leads corresponding with the inferior wall of the heart.

The inferior wall of the left ventricle (LV) is supplied by the posterior descending artery (PDA).  Most patients (ie, approximately 85%) have right-dominant circulation, meaning that the PDA is a branch of the right coronary artery (RCA) as it wraps around the right side of the heart to supply the inferior wall.  The RCA also usually supplies the sinoatrial node (via the sinoatrial nodal branch), such that myocardial infarction involving the RCA often demonstrates sinus bradycardia.

Approximately 10% of patients have left-dominant circulation, meaning that the left circumflex artery (LCx) wraps around the left side of the heart to branch into the PDA and supply the inferior wall.  The remaining 5% of the population has codominant circulation, in which the PDA receives blood from both the RCA and LCx.

(Choices A, B, and C)  The left main coronary artery arises from the aorta and divides into the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the LCx.  The LAD supplies the anterior and septal walls of the LV, and STEMI involving the LAD is expected to demonstrate ST-segment elevation in ECG leads V1 and V2 (septal wall) and/or V3 and V4 (anterior wall),  The LCx supplies the lateral wall of the LV, and STEMI involving the LCx is expected to demonstrate ST-segment elevation in ECG leads V5, V6, I, and aVL; in the small fraction of patients with left-dominant circulation, ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) would also be expected.  STEMI involving the left main coronary artery is a devastating event as it obstructs blood flow to both the LAD and LCx, resulting in widespread myocardial injury.

Educational objective:The inferior wall of the left ventricle is supplied by the posterior descending artery (PDA).  The majority of the population (ie, approximately 85%) has right-dominant circulation, meaning that the PDA is a branch of the right coronary artery (RCA).  Therefore, ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction localized to the inferior ECG leads (II, III, and aVF) usually indicates occlusion of the RCA.​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌
